title: Process boundaries, termination, and recovery
purpose: Find latent correctness failures that appear only when Ledger is started, terminated, killed, and re-executed as a real OS process, including production configuration binding, supervisor-visible exit behavior, kernel-resource ownership, and reopening the same node-local durable state without in-memory continuity.
invariants: Each execution of the production Ledger binary must reconstruct the intended node identity, cluster role, network addresses, storage locations, and supported runtime settings from the documented CLI, environment, and deployment inputs plus durable state; correctness after exec must not depend on memory or process-local state from an earlier execution.

A process must validate supplied configuration and incompatible persisted identity or storage state before reporting readiness or serving externally visible behavior that assumes the configuration is valid; rejected startup must not leave a partially initialized node that a subsequent execution mistakes for a valid first boot or join.

A supported graceful termination signal delivered to the production Ledger process must enter the intended Fx shutdown path, complete process-owned shutdown work within its documented contract, release listeners and storage resources, and expose successful termination to the supervisor only when that contract completes. Internal goroutine ownership and join ordering independent of OS signal delivery remain owned by concurrency-lifecycle-shutdown.

Fatal startup failures and post-start failures that make an owned server or required runtime component unusable must terminate the production process with a non-success status and must not leave it running or externally ready; graceful termination and failure termination must remain distinguishable to process supervisors.

After abrupt process death, acknowledged durable state must be recoverable by a newly executed process opening the same node-local WAL and data paths without relying on shutdown hooks or in-memory cleanup; crash-torn WAL, spool, Pebble, marker, and checkpoint state must be repaired or rejected according to their documented local recovery contracts. Generic durability, replay, snapshot, and restore correctness remains owned by persistence-restore-replay.

Graceful exit, failed startup unwind, and OS-enforced process death must leave kernel-managed listeners and application-managed files, locks, temporary artifacts, and ownership markers in a state that permits a safe immediate re-exec on the same configured endpoints and durable paths, or produces a clear fail-closed error.

Evidence for process restart recovery must prove that a different OS process reopened and validated the intended node-local state. Cluster forwarding, leader reads, snapshot installation, peer repair, or orchestrator replacement may be part of a distributed recovery scenario but must not be accepted as proof of local reopen correctness; Raft quorum, membership, routing, and leadership safety themselves remain owned by raft-membership-leadership, while collection and validation-layer enforcement of process tests remain owned by test-reachability-enforcement.

If process death interrupts persistence-affecting background work, every externally meaningful durable progress state must let a newly executed process resume, retry, roll back, or fail closed without silently publishing incomplete work. This domain owns the hard-death and re-exec boundary; normal cancellation, Stop joining, and worker-generation ownership remain owned by concurrency-lifecycle-shutdown, while the underlying persistence transition remains owned by its subsystem audit.
adversarial_questions: Which production behaviors are exercised only by main.go and the pinned service.Execute/service.App implementation, and which tests instead call Cobra ExecuteContext in a goroutine and stop by cancelling a context? What signal, environment-binding, deferred-cleanup, or exit-code behavior is bypassed in the latter case?

When the real process receives SIGTERM or SIGINT, what causes Fx Stop to run, what exact work must finish before the PID exits, and what status does the parent process or container runtime observe if Stop succeeds, times out, or fails?

Can an invalid environment value, an environment/flag precedence difference, or the operator shell entrypoint reconstruct a node ID, bootstrap/join decision, address, or durable path different from the operator's intent without causing startup to fail clearly?

Can any HTTP, service-gRPC, or Raft listener become reachable, or any readiness signal become positive, before configuration validation, persisted identity/schema validation, local store recovery, and required startup hooks have reached their documented gates?

Can a fatal bind, validation, server-Serve, recovery, or worker-start failure return success, remain hidden behind a running management endpoint, or be converted into a graceful-looking exit by the production entrypoint or a test/container wrapper?

What durable bytes and markers can SIGKILL leave between Raft WAL persistence, committed-entry spooling, Pebble commit, checkpoint publication, and progress-marker advancement, and does a fresh process handle every reachable prefix without shutdown cleanup?

After graceful termination, failed startup, or SIGKILL, can a different PID immediately bind the same three endpoints and reopen every configured Pebble/WAL/cache directory, or can stale locks, inherited descriptors, temporary files, or launcher-owned markers prevent or misdirect restart?

Can a restarted node appear healthy because a request is forwarded to the leader or because a peer installs a snapshot even though the restarted process did not correctly reopen its own committed local state? Which assertions address the restarted node directly with forwarding or peer repair unavailable?

Do restart tests prove PID replacement, preservation of the exact WAL/data paths or PVCs, and a node-local sentinel across the replacement, or can a test named restart execute only an in-process Stop/Start cycle, observe an old PID, or validate only cluster-level availability?

When a leader or follower process is killed and re-executed, which observations establish process-boundary recovery separately from the Raft domain's quorum, membership, leadership-transfer, catch-up, and routing guarantees?

Can hard death during sealing, archival, cache or query checkpointing, projection indexing, usage aggregation, backup orchestration, or cold-cache activity leave a durable progress marker that suppresses necessary work or publishes incomplete work after the new process starts?

Do Schemathesis, the local model runner, operator/Chainsaw, and Antithesis wait for and assert the Ledger process's own termination and replacement outcomes, or only clean up a child/container and later observe an orchestrator-managed service?
dynamic_checks_to_consider: build and spawn the production Ledger binary with isolated fixed WAL/data directories and kernel-assigned endpoints, record its PID, send SIGTERM, wait for the exact child status, and immediately exec a new PID on the same resources
commit a node-local sentinel, send SIGKILL without invoking Stop, wait for the exact child death, re-exec on the same WAL/data paths, and verify the sentinel directly on that process

repeat abrupt death at instrumented WAL append, spool append/replay, Pebble commit, checkpoint publication, and progress-marker boundaries, then classify the fresh process outcome as recover, repair, or explicit fail-closed rejection

start with equivalent supported CLI and environment configurations, including explicit zero values and malformed environment values, and compare the reconstructed configuration, readiness behavior, diagnostics, and process status

attempt startup with mismatched persisted node/cluster identity, incompatible storage schema, occupied listeners, and invalid TLS/auth files; assert no endpoint becomes ready and the process exits non-zero

in a multi-node run, kill and re-exec both follower and leader PIDs while preserving their local volumes, then verify PID replacement, local integrity/state with forwarding disabled, and cluster recovery as separate assertions
hold peers unavailable during a restarted node's local verification so snapshot installation, leader forwarding, and quorum reads cannot mask a broken local reopen path

interrupt sealing, archival, cache/query checkpointing, projection builders, usage aggregation, backup work, and cold-cache population with SIGKILL at deterministic barriers, then re-exec and verify durable progress is resumed, retried, rolled back, or rejected according to the owning subsystem contract

run the production container entrypoint as PID 1, exercise graceful and zero-grace container termination, and assert signal delivery, exit status, persistent-volume reuse, listener reuse, and a new container/PID identity
